overview: Kalinga was an influential eastern Indian region with royal centres, farming communities and trade connections. This card focuses on early historic life around Odisha, especially excavated Sisupalgarh. The imported 1 BCE to 400 CE span is not one dynasty’s lifetime. Its outline is grossly overbroad, reaching north across the Ganges to include Patna; it should not be read as demonstrated Kalinga control. Earlier Kharavela evidence is identified as background, and later Kalinga and Orissa records remain separate.

periods.title: Early historic urban communities
periods.summary: Sisupalgarh participated in wider networks of cities, crafts and exchange. The imported interval describes map coverage rather than a documented continuous reign.

items.text: Before this map slice, King Kharavela advertised his achievements in the seventeen-line Hathigumpha inscription near Bhubaneswar. He is commonly placed in the first century BCE, although the chronology remains debated. Damage makes parts of this royal praise-text difficult to interpret.

The inscription credits Kharavela with repairing storm-damaged gates and walls, improving water facilities and organizing music, dance and festive gatherings. These are a king’s claims about good government, not independent accounts from every household. They nevertheless show that royal reputation could depend on keeping a city usable and entertaining as well as commanding an army.

Sisupalgarh had a roughly square enclosure with eight main gateways, two on each side. At the excavated western gateway, a broad main passage had controlled entry points, while a smaller passage could admit pedestrians when the main gates were shut. Even an ancient city needed a way to let someone walk home without opening the big doors.

Talapada, about 40 kilometres southwest of Sisupalgarh, copied the larger city’s formal ramparts and gateways. Its comparatively thin deposits and lightly developed defences suggest that it never filled with people as densely as planned. Archaeologists use the contrast to investigate why some early historic towns attracted lasting communities while others grew less successfully.

Terracotta pendants with Roman-looking portraits occur at Sisupalgarh and other Odisha sites. They suggest the movement of images and goods through trading networks. A 2019 reassessment found no secure proof of direct Roman shipping to Odisha, and identified a supposed imported amphora fragment as a much later jar. An object can travel through several traders before reaching its wearer.

sections.title: Homes, food and things people wore

items.text: Excavators uncovered Sisupalgarh houses with laterite-stone foundations, earth walls and verandas facing the street. One large example measured about 7.5 by 10 metres; smaller buildings sometimes reused brick and stone. Roof tiles survive even where the wooden supports have vanished. These remains give a household a shape, although they cannot tell us exactly who slept in each room.

Charred rice grains and fish remains came from waterlogged deposits at Sisupalgarh, including layers earlier than this map interval. They show how closely food supplies were tied to a wet landscape. Researchers suggest rice fields may also have supported fish production, but deliberately raising fish there remains an interpretation rather than something the bones alone prove.

A study of animal remains from the 2005 to 2009 excavations found that residents used a wide range of wild and domestic animals early in the city’s history, with less variety later. The researcher interprets that change as consistent with growing religious concern for nonviolence. It does not establish that every household became vegetarian or ate the same meals.

Clay jewellery could be surprisingly elaborate. A published study counted 164 terracotta bangle pieces from Sisupalgarh, with eye-like, floral, rope and other designs; many ornaments were worn and later redeposited in rubbish or building fill. Broken accessories have become evidence for craftspeople’s skills and the fashions people chose to put on their bodies.

The same study catalogued 470 ear ornaments, mostly terracotta. Shapes included pegs, crescents, discs and reels, with parallels as far away as the Ganges valley and Tamil Nadu. Imagine choosing between a little crescent and a tiny spool for your ears. Similar fashions connect places, but do not tell us the wearer’s name, age or gender.

Stone grinding tools from Sisupalgarh included nonlocal chromite, while beads used materials such as carnelian, agate and jasper. Iron implements included sickles, knives and nails. A small pot containing broken bangles and wire suggests that usable metal was being saved. A scrap collection could be tomorrow’s raw material.

sections.title: Water, learning and rediscovering a city

items.text: Reservoirs and wells inside Sisupalgarh reduced the need to go outside the ramparts for water. Excavators explain that these supplies would have been particularly valuable in dry weather or a siege. Fetching water remained practical household work. These discoveries establish water storage and access; they do not establish that every home had a private toilet or sewer.

Electrical and magnetic surveys helped researchers trace buried streets leading inward from the eight gateways. The instruments detected differences underground without first exposing entire neighbourhoods. Survey patterns then guided archaeological interpretation and digging. A field that looked fairly ordinary at the surface could conceal the outline of an ancient street below it.

Modern excavation had a soggy problem: the water table had risen above the deepest ancient layers. Local well-diggers on the research team helped archaeologists use pumps to keep working. Their practical knowledge made it possible to investigate pottery and deposits otherwise hidden underwater. Research here depended on neighbours’ expertise as well as university training.

Kharavela’s earlier inscription praises his preparation for kingship through correspondence, currency, finance and legal knowledge. It offers a glimpse of the education considered suitable for a prince. It is not a school register for ordinary children, whose lessons and family routines are much harder to reconstruct from the surviving evidence.

A short Prakrit sample from Kharavela’s earlier inscription is “Namo Arihantānāṁ”, translated by its editors as “Salutation to the Arhats”. The stone uses Brahmi script; the spelling shown here is the scholarly Latin-letter transcription, not a drawing of its ancient letters. This Jain invocation belongs to a particular royal monument, not every person in Kalinga.

ending.text: The map stops at 400 CE without documenting a single conquest or collapse. Sisupalgarh’s urban role changed, while a new settlement developed nearby from about the sixth century. Researchers interpret the wider Bhubaneswar landscape as a succession of connected urban places. A city’s declining importance did not mean that Kalinga’s communities or regional traditions disappeared.
